questions.q: What is the actual relationship between an application object and a service principal object in Entra ID?
options: They are the same object, just referred to by two different names depending on the Azure portal blade
The service principal is created only if the application object has no credentials configured
The application object is deprecated and only service principals are used in current tenants
The application object is the global, tenant-independent definition; the service principal is the tenant-local identity that actually authenticates and holds RBAC assignments
questions.explain: Every app registration creates both objects. In a multi-tenant app, one application object produces a separate service principal in every consenting tenant.

questions.q: Why are federated credentials (workload identity federation) generally preferred over client secrets for a service principal?
options: They allow a service principal to bypass RBAC scoping entirely
They exchange an external OIDC token for an Entra ID token with no secret stored anywhere, eliminating the leak and rotation problem entirely
They are required by Azure Policy for every app registration regardless of use case
They only work for system-assigned managed identities, not service principals
questions.explain: Federated credentials let an external workload present its own OIDC token in exchange for an Entra ID token, so there is no stored secret to leak or rotate.

questions.q: What is the key practical difference between a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity?
options: User-assigned identities can only be used by virtual machines, never by Azure Functions or App Service
System-assigned identities can be attached to multiple resources simultaneously, user-assigned cannot
A system-assigned identity's lifecycle is tied 1:1 to the resource it's attached to; a user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to multiple resources
User-assigned identities require a client secret, while system-assigned identities do not
questions.explain: System-assigned identities are created and destroyed with their one resource. User-assigned identities exist independently and can be shared across many resources.

questions.q: A managed identity needs to read secrets from exactly one Key Vault. What is the correct way to scope its access?
options: Assign it Key Vault Secrets User, scoped to that one Key Vault
Assign it Contributor on the entire subscription so it never hits a permissions error
Assign it Owner on the resource group containing the Key Vault
Leave it with no RBAC role, since managed identities bypass RBAC by design
questions.explain: The narrowest role at the narrowest scope that satisfies the actual job bounds the blast radius if that workload is ever compromised.

questions.q: Why are client secrets described in this lesson as the last-resort credential type for a service principal?
options: Because Entra ID has fully deprecated client secrets and they no longer function
Because they are a plain string that's easy to leak into source control or CI logs, and a common root cause of real service principal compromises
Because client secrets can only be used with user-assigned managed identities
Because client secrets cannot be stored in Azure Key Vault
questions.explain: Unlike a certificate's private key or a federated credential's tokenless exchange, a client secret is plain text that's easy to accidentally expose, and incident patterns show it's a frequent compromise vector.
